item.title: How to Fix Slow WiFi at Home: A Practical Guide
item.description: Slow WiFi ruining your Netflix nights? Learn how to diagnose and fix common home WiFi problems with simple, actionable steps that actually work.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

You know the feeling. You’re halfway through a movie, the buffer wheel starts spinning, and suddenly your smart TV is displaying a pixelated mess. Or worse — you’re on a video call for work, and your voice starts sounding like a robot underwater.

Last month, my neighbor knocked on my door asking why her WiFi was “broken.” She’d already called her internet provider twice. They told her everything looked fine on their end. Twenty minutes in her apartment, I found the culprit: her router was sitting inside a closed wooden cabinet, next to a microwave, behind a fish tank. Three simple changes later, her speed test went from 8 Mbps to 220 Mbps.

Most slow WiFi problems aren’t actually problems with your internet provider. They’re problems inside your home. Here’s how to find and fix them.

First, Run a Proper Speed Test

Before you change anything, you need a baseline. Go to a speed test site or app and run a test on a device connected directly to your router with an Ethernet cable, if possible. Then run the same test on WiFi from the same spot.

If the wired speed is fast and WiFi is slow, the problem is your wireless setup — not your internet plan. That’s good news, because it’s usually fixable for free.

Test in multiple rooms too. If one room is slow and another is fine, you’ve got a coverage problem, not a speed problem. Those require different solutions.

Router Placement: The Most Overlooked Fix

Your router’s location matters more than almost anything else. WiFi signals are radio waves, and radio waves don’t like obstacles.

Avoid these placements:

  • Inside cabinets, closets, or behind furniture
  • Next to microwaves, cordless phones, or baby monitors (these interfere with the 2.4 GHz band)
  • On the floor or in a basement corner
  • Near fish tanks or large metal objects

Better placement:

  • Central location in your home
  • Elevated — on a shelf or mounted on a wall
  • Out in the open with clear space around it

Think of it like a light bulb. Where would you put a lamp if you wanted to light up your whole house? That’s roughly where your router should go.

Switch to the 5 GHz Band (If You Haven’t Already)

Most modern routers broadcast two networks: 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz. The 2.4 GHz band travels farther but is slower and more crowded. The 5 GHz band is much faster but has shorter range.

If your devices are close to the router, connect them to the 5 GHz network. You’ll often see an immediate, dramatic speed increase. Streaming devices, gaming consoles, and laptops in the same room as the router should almost always be on 5 GHz.

If your router uses “band steering” (one network name for both bands), it may be putting your devices on the wrong band. Check your router settings to see if you can split them into separate names.

Update Your Router’s Firmware

Router manufacturers regularly release firmware updates that fix bugs, improve performance, and patch security holes. Many people never update their router, running firmware that’s years out of date.

Log into your router’s admin panel (usually by typing something like 192.168.1.1 into your browser), find the firmware or update section, and check for updates. Some routers do this automatically — make sure that setting is turned on.

Change Your WiFi Channel

In apartment buildings and dense neighborhoods, everyone’s WiFi is fighting for the same channels. It’s like a crowded highway with too many cars.

For the 2.4 GHz band, only channels 1, 6, and 11 don’t overlap with each other. If your neighbors are all on channel 6, switching to 1 or 11 can help.

You can scan nearby networks using a free app like WiFi Analyzer (Android) or the built-in tools on most computers. Look for the least crowded channel and switch to it in your router settings.

On 5 GHz, this is less of an issue since there are far more channels available.

Reduce Interference and Clutter

Every device in your home that emits radio waves is potentially interfering with your WiFi. That includes:

  • Bluetooth speakers and headphones
  • Wireless security cameras
  • Smart home devices
  • Older cordless phones

You don’t need to get rid of these, but keep them away from your router. A few feet of distance can make a real difference.

Consider a Mesh System or Extender

If your home is large, has thick walls, or has multiple floors, a single router may simply not be enough. This is where mesh WiFi systems shine.

A mesh system uses multiple units placed around your home that work together to create one seamless network. Unlike old-school extenders, mesh systems don’t require you to manually switch networks as you move around.

They’re not cheap — expect to spend $150 to $400 for a good system — but for larger homes, they’re often the single most effective upgrade you can make.

If your budget is tight, a traditional WiFi extender can help, but placement is critical. Put it roughly halfway between your router and the dead zone, not in the dead zone itself.

Check What’s Eating Your Bandwidth

Sometimes your WiFi isn’t slow — it’s just being used up. Common bandwidth hogs include:

  • 4K video streaming (uses up to 25 Mbps per stream)
  • Cloud backups running in the background
  • Large game downloads
  • Someone else’s video calls

Log into your router and look at connected devices. You might find a neighbor using your network (change that password), or a forgotten device downloading updates.

When to Call Your Provider

If you’ve tried everything above and your wired speed is also slow, the problem is likely on your provider’s end. Call them with your speed test results ready. Be specific: “I’m paying for 300 Mbps and getting 40 Mbps on a wired connection.”

That’s a much more effective conversation than “my internet is slow.”

A Quick Checklist

Before you spend money on new gear, run through this list:

  1. Move your router to a central, open, elevated spot
  2. Connect nearby devices to the 5 GHz band
  3. Update your router’s firmware
  4. Change your WiFi channel
  5. Move interfering devices away from the router
  6. Check for bandwidth hogs on your network
  7. Test again

Most people find that steps 1 through 3 solve the majority of their problems. If they don’t, you’ll at least know exactly what’s wrong — and that makes it much easier to fix.

item.title: How to Fix a Slow Internet Connection: 12 Real Solutions
item.description: Slow internet ruining your day? Learn how to diagnose and fix a slow connection with practical steps, from router placement to DNS tweaks.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

Last Tuesday, my neighbor called me in a panic. Her video calls kept freezing mid-sentence, and her kids were threatening mutiny over buffering cartoons. She’d already done the thing everyone does — unplugged the router, waited thirty seconds, plugged it back in. Nothing changed.

When I walked into her house, I spotted the problem in about ten seconds. Her router was sitting on the floor behind a fish tank, sandwiched between a cordless phone base and a microwave. Three of the worst possible neighbors for a Wi-Fi signal, all in one corner.

I moved the router to a bookshelf in the hallway, changed one setting in her router’s admin panel, and her speed test jumped from 4 Mbps to 68 Mbps. No new equipment. No service call. Ten minutes of work.

That’s the thing about slow internet — the fix is often simpler than you think, but only if you diagnose the right problem. Here’s how to actually do that.

First, Figure Out What “Slow” Really Means

Before you touch anything, run a speed test at speedtest.net or fast.com. Write down three numbers: download speed, upload speed, and ping (latency).

Now compare those numbers to what you’re paying for. If you’re on a 300 Mbps plan and getting 280 Mbps, your internet isn’t slow — your problem is somewhere else, like a specific app, a weak Wi-Fi signal in one room, or a device that’s struggling. If you’re paying for 300 Mbps and getting 15 Mbps, you have a genuine connection problem.

This distinction matters because it saves you from wasting an hour rebooting things that were never broken.

The Wired vs. Wireless Test

This is the single most useful diagnostic step, and most people skip it.

Plug a laptop directly into your router with an Ethernet cable. Run the speed test again.

  • Wired speed is fast, Wi-Fi is slow: Your internet service is fine. The problem is your Wi-Fi — signal strength, interference, or router placement.
  • Both are slow: The problem is your modem, your router, your ISP, or the wiring coming into your house.

Knowing which side of that line you’re on cuts your troubleshooting in half.

Fixes for Wi-Fi Problems

Move Your Router (Seriously)

Routers broadcast signal outward and downward. Putting one on the floor, in a closet, or behind a TV is like putting a speaker under a blanket. Ideal placement:

  • Central location in your home, as high as practical
  • Away from metal objects, fish tanks, mirrors, and thick concrete walls
  • At least a few feet from microwaves, cordless phone bases, and baby monitors — all of which operate on or near the 2.4 GHz band

If your router has external antennas, point them vertically for single-story coverage, or angle one horizontally if you need to reach an upstairs room.

Switch to the 5 GHz Band

Most modern routers broadcast two networks: 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz. The 2.4 GHz band travels farther but is slower and more crowded. The 5 GHz band is much faster but has shorter range.

If you’re in the same room as the router and still getting slow speeds, you’re probably connected to 2.4 GHz. Go into your device’s Wi-Fi settings and connect to the network name with “5G” in it. It’s often a bigger jump than upgrading your plan.

Change Your Wi-Fi Channel

In apartment buildings and dense neighborhoods, everyone’s router is shouting on the same channel. It’s like trying to have a conversation in a crowded restaurant.

Log into your router’s admin page (usually 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1), find the wireless channel setting, and switch from “Auto” to a specific channel. For 2.4 GHz, stick to channels 1, 6, or 11 — these don’t overlap. For 5 GHz, most routers handle this well automatically, but you can experiment.

Not sure which channels are crowded? Apps like WiFi Analyzer (Android) or NetSpot (Mac/Windows) show you a visual map of every network around you.

Check for Bandwidth Hogs

One device can ruin everyone’s connection. A 4K Netflix stream eats about 25 Mbps. A cloud backup running in the background can saturate an entire household. Windows updates, game downloads, and security cameras uploading footage all compete for the same pipe.

Log into your router and look at connected devices. If something unfamiliar is there, someone might be piggybacking on your network. Change your Wi-Fi password and use WPA3 encryption if your router supports it.

Fixes for Wired and Modem Problems

Restart in the Right Order

The classic “unplug it and plug it back in” works, but the order matters:

  1. Unplug both the modem and router.
  2. Wait a full 60 seconds (not 10 — capacitors need time to discharge).
  3. Plug in the modem first and wait for all its lights to stabilize.
  4. Then plug in the router.

Doing it out of order can leave your router holding onto a stale IP address.

Check Your Modem’s Signal Levels

If you have cable internet, your modem’s admin page shows downstream and upstream power levels. Downstream should typically be between -15 dBmV and +15 dBmV, and upstream between 37 and 48 dBmV. Values outside those ranges usually mean a wiring or line problem that only your ISP can fix — but at least you’ll know what to tell them when you call.

Ask Your ISP for a New Modem

If you’re renting an older modem from your provider, you might be capped below your plan’s speed without realizing it. A DOCSIS 3.0 modem can’t deliver gigabit speeds; you need DOCSIS 3.1. Ask your ISP whether your equipment actually supports the plan you’re paying for. Sometimes the answer is no, and they’ll swap it for free.

Quick Wins That Often Get Overlooked

Change Your DNS Servers

DNS translates website names into IP addresses. Slow or overloaded DNS servers make every page feel sluggish even when your raw speed is fine. Try switching to Cloudflare (1.1.1.1) or Google (8.8.8.8) in your router settings. It takes two minutes and sometimes produces a noticeable improvement in page load times.

Update Your Router’s Firmware

Router manufacturers quietly release firmware updates that fix performance bugs and security holes. Log into your router’s admin panel and check for updates. If your router is more than five or six years old and hasn’t seen an update in years, it may simply be time for a replacement — modern mesh systems start around $100 and often outperform older flagship routers.

Test at Different Times of Day

If your internet is fast at 7 AM and crawling at 8 PM, the problem isn’t your equipment. That’s congestion on your ISP’s network, and it’s a strong argument for calling them and documenting the pattern. Some providers will credit your bill if they can’t deliver advertised speeds during peak hours.

When to Call Your ISP

Call them when:

  • Wired speeds are consistently well below your plan
  • Your modem’s signal levels are out of range
  • Speeds tank at the same time every day
  • You’ve replaced or ruled out your own equipment

When you call, lead with data: “I’m paying for 500 Mbps, I’ve tested directly wired to the modem, and I’m getting 40 Mbps at 8 PM every night.” That gets you past the script and to a technician who can actually help.

The Bottom Line

Most slow internet problems come down to one of four things: bad router placement, the wrong Wi-Fi band, a bandwidth hog, or outdated equipment. Work through them in that order, and you’ll fix the majority of issues without spending a dime.

And if you take nothing else from this article, take this: run the wired test first. It tells you whether you’re fighting your Wi-Fi or your internet provider — and those are two very different fights.

item.title: How to Improve Home WiFi Signal: 11 Fixes That Actually Work
item.description: Dead zones got you down? Learn 11 proven, practical ways to boost your home WiFi signal—from router placement to channel settings. No jargon, just results.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

Let’s paint a picture. It’s Friday night. You’ve got popcorn, a 4K stream queued up, and your couch is perfectly positioned. You hit play. The spinner of doom appears. You wait. It buffers. You sigh. Then, your phone—sitting right next to the router—loads a 4-second YouTube video instantly.

Sound familiar?

I spent three years living in a 1920s brick bungalow that was essentially a Faraday cage for wireless signals. I tried everything short of running Ethernet cables through the heating vents. After dozens of experiments, router resets, and a few very frustrated calls to my ISP, I learned that fixing WiFi isn’t about magic. It’s about physics, geometry, and a few settings most people never touch.

Here are the 11 actionable fixes that finally turned my dead zones into full-bars zones. I’m not going to tell you to “just buy a new router” right away—that’s the lazy advice. Let’s get technical, but practical.

The Obvious (But Most Ignored) Fix: Router Placement

Stop Hiding Your Router in the Closet

I get it. Routers are ugly. They have blinking lights and antennas that look like a robotic spider. So, we shove them behind the TV, on the floor, or inside a wooden cabinet. This is the #1 reason your WiFi sucks.

WiFi signals are essentially radio waves. They radiate outward in a sphere (unless you have directional antennas). If you put that sphere inside a metal box (your entertainment center) or on the floor, you are cutting the signal off at the knees.

The Fix: Your router needs to be:

  • Elevated: At least 5-6 feet off the ground. Think chest height. This mimics the height of your devices (laptops, phones).
  • Central: Place it as close to the exact center of your home as possible. If your router is in the front bedroom, the back kitchen will always suffer.
  • In the Open: Don’t put it behind your TV. The metal components in the TV will absorb the signal. Don’t put it next to a fish tank (water absorbs 2.4GHz signals like crazy).

Real Example: My buddy had a router in his basement office. The living room (one floor up) had 1 bar. We moved the router to a hallway bookshelf on the main floor. It took 10 minutes. His speeds in the living room went from 5 Mbps to 120 Mbps. No new hardware needed.

The Technical Fix: Change Your Channel (It’s Not a Ghost Town)

Your router broadcasts on a specific channel. By default, most routers are set to “Auto.” The problem? Your neighbors’ routers are also on “Auto,” and they all pile onto the same channels (usually 1, 6, or 11 for 2.4GHz).

Imagine a 10-lane highway. Everyone is crammed into lanes 1, 6, and 11, while lanes 2-5 are empty. That’s your WiFi.

The Fix:

  1. Download a free app like WiFi Analyzer (Android) or NetSpot (Mac/Windows).
  2. Walk around your house and see which channels are congested.
  3. Log into your router admin panel (usually 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1).
  4. Find the “Wireless Settings” section.
  5. Manually set the channel to the least congested one.

Pro Tip: For the 2.4GHz band, only use channels 1, 6, or 11. They don’t overlap. Setting it to channel 3 is a rookie mistake that causes interference.

Separate the Bands: The “Smart Connect” Trap

Modern routers are dual-band (2.4GHz and 5GHz). Many have a feature called “Smart Connect” or “Band Steering” that merges them into one SSID (network name). The theory is great—your device picks the best band. The reality is that older devices (or cheap smart home gadgets) will cling to the 2.4GHz band like a life raft, dragging down the whole network.

The Fix: Log into your router and disable Smart Connect. Give the 2.4GHz network a name like “MyHome_2.4” and the 5GHz network “MyHome_5G”.

  • Use 2.4GHz for: Long range, smart plugs, thermostats, and devices that don’t need speed.
  • Use 5GHz for: Laptops, phones, streaming sticks, and gaming consoles.

This simple split prevents slow devices from bottlenecking your fast devices. It’s the single most effective software tweak I’ve ever made.

Upgrade Your Firmware (Yes, Routers Need Updates Too)

This sounds boring, but it’s crucial. Router manufacturers constantly patch security holes and, more importantly, fix performance bugs. Your router might be running software from 2019 that has known memory leaks.

The Fix: Check your router manufacturer’s app or the admin panel for a “Firmware Update” section. Do this every 3-4 months. It takes 5 minutes and can fix intermittent dropouts that you thought were caused by your ISP.

The Copper Bullet: Use Ethernet for the Heavy Lifters

WiFi is convenient, but it’s half-duplex—it can only send or receive at one time. Ethernet is full-duplex. If you have a stationary device that eats bandwidth (like a Smart TV or a gaming console), plug it in with a cable.

The Fix: Run a single Ethernet cable from your router to your TV. This frees up massive amounts of wireless bandwidth for your phones and tablets. You don’t need to wire the whole house—just the top 2 bandwidth hogs.

Actionable Tip: If you can’t run a cable through walls, use a MOCA adapter (Ethernet over coax) if you have cable TV wiring, or a powerline adapter (Ethernet over electrical wiring). These aren’t as fast as direct Ethernet, but they are more stable than WiFi for gaming.

The Antenna Geometry Lesson

If your router has external antennas, you’re leaving performance on the table if they’re all pointing straight up.

The Fix:

  • Single story home: Point one antenna straight up, and one antenna horizontally (parallel to the floor). This creates a better vertical and horizontal coverage pattern.
  • Two-story home: Point one antenna up, one to the left (horizontal), and one to the right (horizontal). This spreads the signal across multiple floors.

The “Reboot” Schedule

I know, “turn it off and on again” is a cliché. But routers have a finite amount of memory. Over time, they get clogged with stale routing tables and connection states. This causes latency spikes and slow speeds.

The Fix: Don’t wait for it to break. Plug your router and modem into a smart plug and set a schedule to reboot them at 4:00 AM every Sunday. This clears the memory and keeps the network fresh. It costs $10 for a smart plug and saves you hours of frustration.

When to Give Up and Buy a Mesh System

If you’ve done all the above and you still have dead zones in a house larger than 2,000 square feet, stop buying range extenders. Seriously. Range extenders (repeaters) are the worst invention. They halve your bandwidth because they receive and re-transmit on the same channel.

The Fix: Invest in a Mesh WiFi system (like Eero, Google Nest WiFi, or TP-Link Deco). These use dedicated wireless backhaul channels to talk to each other, so your devices get the full speed. They also handle handoff better, so you don’t drop your video call when you walk from the kitchen to the office.

My Experience: I switched to a 3-node mesh system two years ago. My 1,800 sq ft bungalow went from having 2 dead zones to having 100% coverage. The setup took 15 minutes via an app. It’s the only hardware upgrade that truly solved the problem.

The Hidden Culprit: Interference from Neighbors (DFS Channels)

If you live in an apartment or a dense neighborhood, your 5GHz band is probably just as congested as your 2.4GHz band. However, there are channels called DFS (Dynamic Frequency Selection) that share spectrum with weather/military radar. Most routers avoid these by default because they require the router to listen for radar and switch channels if needed.

The Fix: In your router settings, look for “DFS Channels” or “Enable 802.11h”. Enabling this opens up a ton of extra channels that your neighbors aren’t using. The downside is that if a radar signal is detected, your WiFi will briefly drop to switch channels. For most suburban homes, this is a non-issue, and the speed increase is massive.

Check Your Cables (The Weakest Link)

This is the one people hate. You have gigabit internet, but you’re using a 15-year-old Ethernet cable that is Cat5 (not Cat5e). That cable can only handle 100 Mbps.

The Fix: Check the printing on your Ethernet cables. If it says “Cat5” without an “e” or a “6”, replace it. Also, ensure your coax cable (the one from the wall to your modem) is tightly screwed in and not frayed. A loose coax connection is the #1 cause of intermittent “modem offline” errors.

The Final Step: Call Your ISP (But Be Prepared)

If you’ve optimized everything and your speeds are still terrible, it might be a signal issue from the street. But before you call, run a speed test with a laptop plugged directly into the modem via Ethernet.

  • If the wired speed is good (close to your plan), the issue is your WiFi (which we just fixed).
  • If the wired speed is bad, it’s your ISP.

The Script: “I’ve tested hardwired to the modem and I’m only getting X Mbps when I pay for Y. Can you check the signal levels at the tap?” They can see your signal-to-noise ratio remotely. Often, they’ll send a tech to fix a corroded connector outside your house—which is free.

Conclusion

Improving your WiFi isn’t about buying the most expensive gear. It’s about being methodical. Start with placement (free), then move to channel settings (free), then split your bands (free), and only then consider spending money.

I promise you, if you take 30 minutes today to move your router off the floor and change your channels, you’ll see a noticeable difference tonight. Don’t chase the “latest WiFi 7” hype until you’ve mastered the basics. Your network is probably 80% capable of what you want—you just need to unblock it. Good luck, and enjoy the buffer-free streaming.

item.title: Fix WiFi Connection Issues: 7 Steps That Actually Work
item.description: Tried everything and your WiFi still drops? Here’s a no-nonsense guide to diagnosing and fixing common home network problems.
item.content:encoded:
TITLE: Fix WiFi Connection Issues: 7 Steps That Actually Work DESCRIPTION: Tried everything and your WiFi still drops? Here’s a no-nonsense guide to diagnosing and fixing common home network problems. TAGS: WiFi troubleshooting, fix internet connection, home network tips, router setup, slow WiFi fix

Introduction

You’re in the middle of a video call, and suddenly the screen freezes. The dreaded spinning wheel appears. Your colleague’s voice cuts out. You check your phone—two bars, but nothing loads. Sound familiar?

WiFi issues are the modern equivalent of a clogged drain. They’re frustrating, they happen at the worst possible moment, and most people either restart the router or call their ISP. But here’s the thing: most WiFi problems are fixable in under ten minutes with a little systematic thinking.

I’ve spent years setting up networks for small offices and homes, and I’ve seen the same handful of culprits over and over. This guide walks through the real fixes—not “try turning it off and on again” (though yes, that does sometimes work). Let’s get your connection back.

The Quick Checklist Before You Panic

Before diving into router settings or buying new equipment, run through these three things. They solve about 40% of all WiFi issues.

Check if it’s just you. Can other devices in your home load websites? If your phone works but your laptop doesn’t, the problem is the laptop, not the WiFi. Try forgetting the network and reconnecting, or check if airplane mode got turned on accidentally.

Restart your modem and router in the right order. Unplug both. Wait 30 seconds. Plug in the modem first. Wait until all lights are solid (usually 1–2 minutes). Then plug in the router. This forces a clean handshake between your ISP and your home network. Doing it in reverse order often causes the router to grab a bad IP address.

Check for an outage. Call your ISP’s automated line or check downdetector.com. Sometimes the problem isn’t your equipment—it’s a cut fiber line three blocks away.

Step 1: Find the Physical Culprit

WiFi is radio waves. Radio waves hate metal, concrete, water, and thick walls. Your router might be in the worst possible spot.

Where is your router right now? If it’s behind your TV, inside a cabinet, or on the floor next to a fish tank, move it. The ideal spot is:

  • Elevated – on a shelf or desk, not the floor
  • Central – as close to the middle of your home as possible
  • Clear – away from large metal objects (refrigerators, filing cabinets, mirrors)

I once spent an hour troubleshooting a client’s slow WiFi before noticing their router was sitting directly on top of a microwave. Every time they reheated coffee, the network dropped. Move the router three feet away, and the problem vanished.

Check your ethernet cable too. A damaged or loose cable between your modem and router causes intermittent drops. If the cable is pinched under furniture or looks chewed (pets love these), replace it. It’s a $5 fix.

Step 2: Stop Channel Congestion

Your WiFi broadcasts on a specific channel, like a radio station. In apartment buildings or dense neighborhoods, your neighbors might be broadcasting on the same channel. This causes interference and slowdowns.

Use a WiFi analyzer app. On Android, WiFi Analyzer (free) shows you which channels are crowded. On Windows, try NirSoft WifiInfoView. On iPhone, you’re limited—try AirPort Utility (enable WiFi scanner in settings) or just use a laptop.

Ideally, you want your router on a channel that no one else is using, or at least one with fewer networks. For 2.4 GHz, channels 1, 6, and 11 are the only ones that don’t overlap. Pick the least crowded of those three.

How to change the channel: Log into your router’s admin panel (typically 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1—check the sticker on the router). Look for “Wireless Settings” or “WiFi Channel.” Change it from “Auto” to a specific channel. Save and reboot.

If your router supports 5 GHz, use it. 5 GHz has more channels, less interference, and faster speeds—but shorter range. For most homes, using both bands (2.4 GHz for range, 5 GHz for speed) is optimal.

Step 3: Update Firmware and Drivers

This is the most overlooked fix. Router manufacturers release firmware updates to fix bugs, security holes, and performance issues. If your router hasn’t been updated in two years, it’s running outdated software.

Router firmware: Log into your admin panel. Look for “Firmware Update” or “Router Update.” Some routers update automatically; most don’t. Download the latest version from the manufacturer’s site if the router doesn’t have a built-in updater.

Network drivers on your computer: On Windows, open Device Manager, find “Network adapters,” right-click your WiFi card, and select “Update driver.” On Mac, they’re usually updated through system updates. Outdated drivers cause random disconnects and slow speeds that aren’t the router’s fault.

Real example: A friend complained that his WiFi dropped every 20 minutes on his Windows laptop. His phone worked fine. I checked his WiFi driver—it was from 2019. Updated it. Problem gone. That’s a 30-second fix.

Step 4: Check for Bandwidth Hogs

Sometimes your WiFi isn’t broken—it’s overloaded. If your internet plan is 100 Mbps and someone is streaming 4K Netflix (about 25 Mbps), someone else is on a Zoom call (5–10 Mbps), and a third person is downloading a game update (50+ Mbps), you’re at capacity.

Log into your router and look at connected devices. Most modern routers have a “Traffic” or “Bandwidth” section. You’ll see which devices are using the most data.

Common culprits:

  • Windows updates downloading in the background
  • Cloud backups (iCloud, Google Drive, OneDrive) syncing large files
  • Smart home devices constantly uploading data
  • BitTorrent or other P2P apps running on someone’s computer

If you see “Unknown Device” using 80% of your bandwidth, change your WiFi password immediately. Someone might be piggybacking on your network.

Step 5: Reset Your Network Settings (The Nuclear Option)

If you’ve tried everything and the problem persists, resetting your network settings can clear out corrupted configurations. This is different from just restarting.

On your computer:

  • Windows: Settings > Network & Internet > Advanced network settings > Network reset. This removes all saved WiFi networks and VPNs. You’ll need to reconnect afterward.
  • Mac: System Settings > Network > Select WiFi > “Renew DHCP Lease” or “Delete Service” and re-add it.

On your router: Find the small pinhole button labeled “Reset.” Press and hold it with a paperclip for 10 seconds (usually while the router is powered on). This wipes all custom settings—SSID, password, port forwards, everything. You’ll need to set it up from scratch.

Don’t confuse “Reset” with “Restart.” Restart just reboots. Reset wipes. Use reset only as a last resort, but it fixes issues that nothing else can.

Step 6: When to Give Up and Buy New Gear

Sometimes the hardware is just too old. If your router is more than 4–5 years old, it might not support modern standards like WiFi 6 (802.11ax). Older routers also have weaker processors and can’t handle multiple devices.

Signs you need a new router:

  • You have more than 10 devices connected and the router feels hot to the touch
  • Speeds are consistently below 50% of what you pay for, even when standing next to the router
  • The router drops connection every few hours, and a restart fixes it temporarily
  • You live in a house over 1,500 square feet and the signal doesn’t reach the far rooms

Consider a mesh system if you have dead zones. Brands like Eero, TP-Link Deco, or Asus ZenWiFi place multiple nodes around your home that talk to each other. They’re easier to set up than traditional routers and handle interference better.

Don’t buy a “gaming router” unless you actually game. Most people just need a solid dual-band router with good range. A $60 TP-Link Archer often outperforms a $200 “premium” router from five years ago.

Step 7: The ISP Call That Actually Works

If you’ve done all the above and still have issues, it’s time to call your internet service provider. But don’t just call and say “my WiFi is slow.” They’ll blame your equipment.

Prepare before you call:

  • Note exactly when the problem happens (every evening at 7 PM? Only on weekends?)
  • Run a speed test while plugged directly into the modem with an ethernet cable. Write down the result.
  • Check your modem’s signal levels. Log into the modem (usually 192.168.100.1) and look for “Downstream Power Level” or “SNR.” Ideally, power should be between -7 and +7 dBmV, and SNR above 30 dB.

When you call, say: “I’m getting X Mbps when hardwired to the modem, but I pay for Y Mbps. Can you check my signal levels and run a line test?” This tells them you’ve done the homework and forces them to actually investigate instead of sending a generic signal refresh.

Final Thoughts

WiFi problems are rarely mysterious. They’re usually caused by one of five things: bad placement, channel interference, outdated drivers, bandwidth overload, or aging hardware. Work through this list in order, and you’ll fix 9 out of 10 issues without spending a dime.

And if you do end up buying a new router, keep the box. Some ISPs require you to return their modem if you replace it, and you’ll want to test the new setup for a week before tossing the old one.

Now go fix that connection. Your next video call depends on it.
